prompt: An electron moves in a circular orbit at constant speed. Why is its linear momentum mv⃗ not constant?

choices.text: The direction of its velocity keeps changing
Its speed rises and falls as it goes round the orbit
choices.why: In this model the speed |v⃗| stays the same. Momentum is a vector, and it changes because the direction of v⃗ keeps turning.

choices.text: The radius of its orbit keeps changing
choices.why: The radius of a circular orbit is fixed. mv⃗ changes because v⃗ points in a new direction at every instant.

choices.text: It is constant; only the energy changes
choices.why: The section says mv⃗ is not constant in circular motion, even at constant speed. It is the energy and the angular momentum that stay constant.

explanation: Velocity is a vector, with a size and a direction. In a circular orbit the speed is constant, but the direction of v⃗ changes all the time, so mv⃗ changes. By Newton's second law a force must act: the nucleus's electrostatic pull.

prompt: In the classical picture of an electron in a circular orbit, which way does the angular momentum vector L⃗ point?

choices.text: Along the rotation axis, perpendicular to the orbit
Along the radius, from the electron to the nucleus
choices.why: That is the direction of the attractive force on the electron. L⃗ points along the axis about which the electron rotates.

choices.text: Along the electron's velocity, tangent to the orbit
choices.why: That is the direction of the linear momentum mv⃗. L⃗ points along the axis of rotation.

choices.text: In the plane of the orbit, turning with the electron
choices.why: L⃗ doesn't turn with the electron. It stays fixed along the axis of rotation, at right angles to the plane of the orbit.

explanation: The angular momentum vector L⃗ is directed along the axis of rotation, at right angles to the plane of the orbit. Its magnitude is |L⃗| = mvr.

prompt: In the classical model, the electron's linear momentum keeps changing, yet its angular momentum stays constant. Why?

choices.text: The force on it acts along r, not along its motion
No force at all acts on the electron in its orbit
choices.why: A force does act: the electrostatic attraction to the nucleus. It points along the radius, so it turns v⃗ without changing L⃗.

choices.text: Its speed keeps changing to make up for it
choices.why: The speed is constant in this model. |L⃗| = mvr stays constant because the force has no component along the direction of motion.

choices.text: No force of any kind can ever change angular momentum
choices.why: A force along v⃗ would change the angular velocity and L⃗; such a force exerts a torque. The nucleus's pull along r exerts none.

explanation: The electrostatic force from the nucleus points along the radius, at right angles to the motion. It changes only the direction of mv⃗, so the speed, the radius and the plane of the orbit, and therefore L⃗, stay constant.

prompt: How are angular momentum and torque related, according to the section?

choices.text: A torque changes L⃗, as a force changes momentum
Torque is just another name for angular momentum
choices.why: They are different quantities. A torque is what changes L⃗, just as a force changes linear momentum.

choices.text: A torque acts only when L⃗ stays constant
choices.why: It's the reverse: when a torque acts, L⃗ changes. With no torque, as in the atom, L⃗ stays constant.

choices.text: Torque is the energy stored in circular motion
choices.why: Torque is not an energy. It plays the part for L⃗ that force plays for linear momentum: it changes it.

explanation: When a force changes L⃗, a torque is said to act on the system. Angular momentum and torque are related in the same way as linear momentum and force. In the atom the force is along r, so there is no torque and L⃗ is constant.

prompt: In the classical model, |L⃗| = mvr. An electron (m = 9.11 × 10^−31 kg) moves at v = 2.19 × 10^6 m/s in a circle of radius r = 5.29 × 10^−11 m. What is |L⃗|, in J·s? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
explanation: |L⃗| = mvr = (9.11 × 10^−31 kg)(2.19 × 10^6 m/s)(5.29 × 10^−11 m) = 1.06 × 10^−34 J·s. This is about the size of ħ = 1.055 × 10^−34 J·s, the natural unit of angular momentum in an atom.

prompt: In the classical model, |L⃗| = mvr. If an electron's speed were halved and the radius of its orbit tripled, by what factor would |L⃗| change? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: |L⃗| is proportional to both v and r, so the new value is (1/2) × 3 = 1.5 times the old one.

prompt: Which quantum number governs the magnitude of an electron's orbital angular momentum?

choices.text: l, the angular momentum quantum number
n, the principal quantum number, as for the energy
choices.why: n sets the energy and limits how large l can be, but the magnitude itself is set by l: |L| = √(l(l + 1))ħ.

choices.text: m_l, the magnetic quantum number
choices.why: m_l gives the z component, L_z = m_l ħ, not the magnitude. The magnitude is set by l.

choices.text: m_s, the spin quantum number
choices.why: m_s describes the electron's spin. The magnitude of the orbital angular momentum is set by l.

explanation: Just as n determines the energy, the quantum number l governs the magnitude of the angular momentum: |L| = √(l(l + 1))ħ, with l = 0, 1, 2, …, n − 1.

prompt: The magnitude of the orbital angular momentum is |L| = √(l(l + 1))ħ. For an electron in a p orbital, |L| is a number times ħ. What is the number?
explanation: A p orbital has l = 1, so |L| = √(1 × 2)ħ = √2 ħ = 1.41ħ. Note that this is larger than ħ: the magnitude is not simply lħ.

prompt: What is the magnitude of the orbital angular momentum of an electron in an s orbital?

choices.text: Zero, because l = 0
√2 ħ, because l = 1 for an s orbital
choices.why: s orbitals have l = 0, not l = 1. With l = 0, |L| = √(0 × 1)ħ = 0.

choices.text: ħ, the smallest amount allowed
choices.why: |L| = √(l(l + 1))ħ, and for an s orbital l = 0, so |L| = 0. There is no smallest nonzero amount that s electrons must have.

choices.text: nħ, so it grows with n for ns orbitals
choices.why: That is Bohr's old rule. In quantum mechanics |L| depends on l, and every s orbital has l = 0, so |L| = 0 whatever n is.

explanation: s orbitals are the states with l = 0, so |L| = √(l(l + 1))ħ = 0. The 1s, 2s, 3s, … orbitals all have zero angular momentum and are told apart by n.

prompt: The value of l can be at most n − 1. What is the smallest value of n that allows g orbitals, which have l = 4?
explanation: l ≤ n − 1 means n ≥ l + 1. For l = 4, n must be at least 4 + 1 = 5, so the first shell with g orbitals is n = 5.

prompt: What does it mean to say that a hydrogen atom's electron is "in" the 2s orbital?

choices.text: The atom is in the quantum state with n = 2 and l = 0
The electron follows a circular path at a fixed radius
choices.why: An orbital is not a path. It is a mathematical function, and being "in" it means being in the quantum state it describes.

choices.text: The electron is held inside a solid shell round the nucleus
choices.why: An orbital has no physical reality of its own; it is a function. The phrase means the atom is in the state that function describes.

choices.text: The electron has two units of angular momentum, 2ħ
choices.why: The 2 is n, not l. A 2s orbital has l = 0, so the electron has no orbital angular momentum.

explanation: An orbital is a mathematical function with no physical reality of its own. Saying the electron is "in" the 2s orbital means the atom is in the quantum state that orbital describes: n = 2 and l = 0.

prompt: Which orbitals have a spherically symmetric electron density?

choices.text: Only s orbitals, which have no angular momentum
All orbitals, since the atom itself is spherical
choices.why: Once the electron has angular momentum (l > 0), its density is no longer spherical; a p orbital has two lobes along an axis.

choices.text: Only p orbitals, since there are three of them
choices.why: A single p orbital is concentrated along one axis, so it is not spherical. Only s orbitals, with l = 0, are.

choices.text: Every orbital with n = 1 or n = 2
choices.why: The 2p orbitals have n = 2 but are not spherical. What matters is l: only l = 0 orbitals are spherical.

explanation: When an electron has angular momentum, its density distribution is no longer spherical. Only s orbitals, with l = 0 and zero angular momentum, give spherical density distributions.

prompt: As an electron's orbital angular momentum increases, how does its density distribution change?

choices.text: It gathers along an axis or in a plane
It becomes more and more nearly spherical
choices.why: Only l = 0 (s) orbitals are spherical. With more angular momentum the density is concentrated more and more along an axis or in a plane.

choices.text: It piles up more and more at the nucleus
choices.why: Orbitals with angular momentum put no density at the nucleus at all; only s orbitals do.

choices.text: It doesn't change; only the energy changes
choices.why: The shape does change: s orbitals are spherical, p orbitals have two lobes along an axis, and d orbitals are more concentrated still.

explanation: Only s electrons, with zero angular momentum, have spherical densities. As the angular momentum increases (p, then d), the density becomes increasingly concentrated along an axis or in a plane in space.

prompt: In three dimensions, what does the electron density of a single 2p orbital look like?

choices.text: Two lobes, one on each side of the nucleus
A sphere centered on the nucleus
choices.why: Spherical density belongs to s orbitals (l = 0). A p electron has angular momentum, so its density is concentrated along an axis.

choices.text: A flat ring lying in the nodal plane
choices.why: The nodal plane is where the density is zero. The density sits in two lobes along the axis, one on each side of that plane.

choices.text: Four lobes arranged in a cross around the nucleus
choices.why: A p orbital has one nodal plane, which splits its density into two lobes. The d orbitals, with two nodes, have more complicated shapes.

explanation: A p orbital's density is concentrated along an axis, in two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, each circular in cross section. The lobes are separated by a nodal plane through the nucleus.

prompt: How does the sign of a 2p wavefunction compare on the two sides of its nodal plane?

choices.text: Positive on one side and negative on the other
The same sign on both sides of the plane
choices.why: The wavefunction changes sign as it passes through the node: it is positive on one side and negative on the other.

choices.text: Positive near the nucleus and negative far from it
choices.why: That would describe a sign change at a spherical (radial) node. The 2p orbital changes sign across its nodal plane instead.

choices.text: Zero on one side and positive on the other
choices.why: The orbital is zero only in the nodal plane itself. On each side it is nonzero, with opposite signs.

explanation: The 2p orbital is positive on one side, and negative on the other side, of the plane through the nucleus that is perpendicular to its axis. It is zero in that plane, which is its node.

prompt: How does the electron density at the nucleus compare for the 1s and 2p orbitals?

choices.text: It is a maximum for 1s and zero for 2p
It is zero for 1s and a maximum for 2p
choices.why: It's the other way round. The 2p nodal plane passes through the nucleus, while the 1s density peaks there.

choices.text: It is zero for both orbitals
choices.why: Only the 2p density is zero there. The 1s density is largest at the nucleus; s orbitals are the only ones that put density at the nucleus.

choices.text: It is the same for both orbitals
choices.why: They differ: the 2p orbital has a node through the nucleus, so its density there is zero, while the 1s density is at its maximum.

explanation: The 2p orbital has a nodal plane through the nucleus, so a 2p electron places no charge density there. The 1s density, by contrast, is greatest at the nucleus. Only s orbitals put density at the nucleus.

prompt: The 2p_z wavefunction is ψ_(2, 1, 0) = zR(r), where the radial part R(r) is never zero at finite r. Where is ψ_(2, 1, 0) equal to zero?

choices.text: Everywhere in the xy-plane
Everywhere along the z axis
choices.why: Along the z axis, z ≠ 0 except at the nucleus, so ψ is not zero there; that is where the lobes point. ψ vanishes where z = 0.

choices.text: Everywhere in the xz-plane
choices.why: The xz-plane is where y = 0, but ψ depends on z, not y. It vanishes where z = 0, the xy-plane.

choices.text: Only at the nucleus itself
choices.why: The nucleus lies in the node, but so does every other point with z = 0. ψ = 0 over the whole xy-plane.

explanation: ψ_(2, 1, 0) = zR(r) is zero wherever z = 0, and z = 0 describes the xy-plane. That plane is the nodal plane of the 2p_z orbital.

prompt: In L_z = m_l ħ, what does the magnetic quantum number m_l give?

choices.text: The component of L along the chosen z axis
The total magnitude of the angular momentum
choices.why: The magnitude is |L| = √(l(l + 1))ħ, set by l. m_l gives only the projection on the z axis.

choices.text: The electron's energy when there is no field
choices.why: Without a magnetic field all m_l values have the same energy. m_l gives the z component, L_z = m_l ħ.

choices.text: The number of radial nodes in the orbital
choices.why: Radial nodes depend on n and l. m_l gives the projection of the angular momentum on the z axis.

explanation: m_l gives the projection of the angular momentum on an arbitrarily chosen direction, called the z direction or quantization axis: L_z = m_l ħ. Loosely, it refers to the direction of the angular momentum vector.

prompt: L_z = m_l ħ, and for a given l, m_l takes the 2l + 1 values −l, …, 0, …, +l. What is the largest possible L_z for an electron in a d orbital (l = 2)? L_z is a number times ħ. What is the number?
explanation: For l = 2, m_l can be −2, −1, 0, +1 or +2. The largest is m_l = +2, so L_z = 2ħ. This is less than the magnitude |L| = √6 ħ = 2.45ħ, so L never points exactly along z.

prompt: When does the value of m_l affect the energy of a hydrogen atom's electron?

choices.text: Only when the atom is in a magnetic field
Always: a larger m_l always means a higher energy
choices.why: Without a magnetic field, all m_l values are equivalent and have the same energy. m_l matters only in a field.

choices.text: Only when the electron is in an s orbital
choices.why: An s orbital has l = 0, so m_l can only be 0 and there is nothing to split. m_l matters only in a magnetic field.

choices.text: Never; m_l has no connection with energy
choices.why: m_l does shift the energy in an external magnetic field. This is the Zeeman effect, which gives m_l its name.

explanation: With no magnetic field, the orbitals with different m_l are equivalent and have the same energy. In an external magnetic field their energies shift by different amounts, the Zeeman effect, which is why m_l is called the magnetic quantum number.

prompt: Besides its orbital angular momentum, what else contributes to the magnetic dipole moment of an electron in an atom?

choices.text: Its spin, described by m_s
The mass of the nucleus
choices.why: The section names the electron's spin, not the nucleus, as the other source of the magnetic moment. Spin has its own quantum number, m_s.

choices.text: Its principal quantum number n
choices.why: n is not a separate source of magnetic moment. The section says the moment comes from the orbital angular momentum and from the spin.

choices.text: Its electrostatic attraction to the nucleus
choices.why: That attraction holds the electron in the atom but gives no magnetic moment. The extra contribution comes from the electron's spin.

explanation: The magnetic dipole moment of an electron in an atomic orbital comes not only from its orbital angular momentum but also from its spin, described by the fourth quantum number, m_s.

prompt: Which of the three 2p orbitals corresponds directly to m_l = 0?

choices.text: 2p_z
2p_x
choices.why: 2p_x is a combination of the m_l = +1 and m_l = −1 functions. The m_l = 0 function is r cos θR(r) = zR(r), which is 2p_z.

choices.text: 2p_y
choices.why: 2p_y is also built from the m_l = +1 and −1 functions. m_l = 0 gives zR(r), the 2p_z orbital.

choices.text: None of them; each one mixes all three m_l values
choices.why: 2p_z is exactly the m_l = 0 function, ψ_(2, 1, 0) = zR(r). Only 2p_x and 2p_y are combinations, of the m_l = +1 and −1 functions.

explanation: ψ_(2, 1, 0) = r cos θR(r), and z = r cos θ, so ψ_(2, 1, 0) = zR(r): the 2p_z orbital. The other two, 2p_x and 2p_y, are combinations of the m_l = +1 and m_l = −1 functions.

prompt: Can the m_l = +1 wavefunction be identified with the 2p_x orbital?

choices.text: No; 2p_x mixes the m_l = +1 and −1 functions
Yes; m_l = +1 is 2p_x and m_l = −1 is 2p_y
choices.why: This is sometimes taught in introductory courses, but it is incorrect. 2p_x and 2p_y are each combinations of the m_l = +1 and −1 functions.

choices.text: Yes; each m_l value matches one axis, x, y or z
choices.why: Only m_l = 0 matches an axis, giving 2p_z. The m_l = ±1 functions contain e^(±iφ), and 2p_x and 2p_y are combinations of them.

choices.text: No; m_l = +1 belongs to a d orbital
choices.why: For l = 1, m_l can be −1, 0 or +1, so m_l = +1 is a p function. It just isn't 2p_x by itself.

explanation: The m_l = ±1 wavefunctions contain e^(±iφ) and are complex. Combining them gives the real functions xf(r) and yf(r), the 2p_x and 2p_y orbitals. Only m_l = 0 corresponds directly to one p orbital, 2p_z.

prompt: Why is it allowed to combine the m_l = +1 and m_l = −1 wavefunctions to make the 2p_x and 2p_y orbitals?

choices.text: The Schrödinger equation is linear
The two functions are orthogonal
choices.why: Orthogonality isn't what allows it. Because the Schrödinger equation is linear, linear combinations of its solutions are solutions too.

choices.text: A magnetic field mixes the two states
choices.why: No field is needed. The combination is allowed because the Schrödinger equation is linear.

choices.text: The two functions are identical
choices.why: They differ: one contains e^(iφ) and the other e^(−iφ). They can be combined because the Schrödinger equation is linear.

explanation: If a set of wavefunctions solves the Schrödinger equation, so does any linear combination of them, because the equation is linear. The m_l = +1 and −1 functions have the same energy, so their combinations 2p_x and 2p_y are solutions with that energy too.

prompt: Which d orbital can be assigned a single value of m_l?

choices.text: d_(z²), with m_l = 0
d_xy, with m_l = +2
choices.why: Like 2p_x and 2p_y, the d orbitals other than d_(z²) are combinations of complex functions, so they have no single m_l value.

choices.text: Every d orbital, with m_l from −2 to +2
choices.why: Only d_(z²) matches one m_l value. The rest are linear combinations of functions with complex angular parts.

choices.text: None of them; d orbitals have no m_l
choices.why: d orbitals do have m_l values, five of them. d_(z²) is the one that corresponds to a single value, m_l = 0.

explanation: As with the p orbitals, only the m_l = 0 function matches one familiar real orbital: d_(z²). The other d orbitals are linear combinations of hydrogen wavefunctions with complex angular parts.

prompt: Where do the orbital labels s, p, d and f come from?

choices.text: Old names for kinds of spectral lines
The shapes: spherical, peanut, dumbbell and flower
choices.why: They are not shape names. s, p, d and f stood for sharp, principal, diffuse and fundamental, words used to describe spectral lines.

choices.text: The initials of the scientists who found them
choices.why: They describe spectral lines, not people: sharp, principal, diffuse and fundamental.

choices.text: They are just the next letters of the alphabet
choices.why: Alphabetical order starts only after f (g, h, i, …). s, p, d and f came from describing spectral lines.

explanation: The labels come from early experimental atomic spectroscopy: s for sharp, p for principal, d for diffuse and f for fundamental. After f the letters run alphabetically: g, h, i, … for l = 4, 5, 6.

prompt: Orbitals with l = 4 are labelled g. There are 2l + 1 orbitals for each value of l. How many g orbitals does a shell that has them contain?
explanation: 2l + 1 = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9 g orbitals, one for each of the 9 values of the angular momentum component (m_l = −4 to +4). Compare 1 s, 3 p, 5 d and 7 f orbitals.

prompt: For n = 4, l can be 0, 1, 2 or 3, and each value of l has 2l + 1 orbitals. How many hydrogen orbitals have n = 4 in all?
explanation: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 orbitals (4s, three 4p, five 4d and seven 4f). This is n^2 = 4^2 = 16, the full degeneracy of the n = 4 level.

prompt: How do the three 2p orbitals of hydrogen differ from one another?

choices.text: Only in how they are oriented in space
In their energy, with 2p_z the lowest
choices.why: With no field, the three 2p orbitals have the same n and l and the same energy. They differ only in orientation.

choices.text: In the magnitude of their angular momentum
choices.why: All three have l = 1, so all have |L| = √2 ħ. They differ in orientation.

choices.text: In shape: one is spherical, two have lobes
choices.why: All three have the same two-lobed shape, since all have l = 1. They point along different directions.

explanation: All orbitals with the same n and l, such as the three 2p orbitals, are similar but differ in their spatial orientations. They have the same energy and the same |L|.
